recent_posts.title: Playwright for .NET apps - Meet Uno Platform's MCP Tools!
recent_posts.summary: Uno Platform introduces MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools that bring Playwright-like automation capabilities to .NET native apps across desktop, mobile, and web. Two MCP servers are provided: one for documentation search and grounding AI agents with up-to-date Uno Platform docs, and another (App MCP) that gives AI agents eyes and hands over running native apps — enabling screenshots, clicks, text input, navigation, and visual tree inspection. This allows developers to validate AI-generated UI code in native .NET apps the same way Playwright does for web apps, supporting iOS, Android, Windows, macOS, Linux, and WebAssembly targets from a single shared codebase.

recent_posts.title: Hidden build performance costs of .NET source generators
recent_posts.summary: Source generators in .NET run on every single build as part of the Roslyn compilation pipeline, not just once. A typical mid-sized solution can have 8–12 active generators, each executing against the full syntax tree. The key distinction is between the original ISourceGenerator (no caching, full cost every build) and IIncrementalGenerator (introduced in .NET 6, caches unchanged outputs). Many popular NuGet packages still ship non-incremental generators. Multi-targeting multiplies costs per target framework, Hot Reload silently falls back to full rebuilds when generators are involved, and IDE IntelliSense suffers continuous background overhead. Practical guidance covers measuring generator cost via MSBuild binary logs and ReportAnalyzer, checking whether a generator is incremental by inspecting its assembly, and mitigation strategies including emitting/caching generated files, isolating generators to dedicated projects, and conditionally disabling them in Debug builds.

recent_posts.title: React UI for ABP Framework Is Finally Here
recent_posts.summary: ABP Framework 10.4.0-rc.1 introduces a long-awaited React UI as a beta/preview option in its modern template system. The implementation includes a Vite-powered React + TypeScript frontend with TanStack Router, TanStack Query, Axios, Zod, React Hook Form, shadcn/ui, Tailwind CSS, and Vitest. The architecture separates the developer's own React app from a pre-built ABP Admin Console (delivered via NuGet) that handles standard module administration pages. The generated app ships with authentication flows, localization, permission-aware routing, API proxy generation, and an optional CRUD sample. It supports layered, single-layer, and microservice templates via the ABP CLI `--modern` flag. The design philosophy keeps actual page code inside the project rather than locked in npm packages, enabling full customization and AI-assisted development. General availability is planned for ABP 10.4 stable.

recent_posts.title: Disable CloudWatch Logs and Cut Your AWS Bill
recent_posts.summary: CloudWatch Logs can significantly inflate AWS bills, especially at high log volumes. By configuring an OpenTelemetry extension to ship logs to a compatible third-party observability provider, you can bypass CloudWatch entirely and reduce costs.

recent_posts.title: .NET 10 file based apps tutorial for running C# scripts without a project
recent_posts.summary: .NET 10 introduces file-based applications, allowing C# scripts to run directly from a single .cs file without creating a project or solution. The tutorial covers how to run a .cs file with `dotnet run`, add NuGet packages using `#:package` directives, configure MSBuild properties like `PublishAot` and language version via `#:property`, use the Web SDK to build a minimal API from a single file, publish the app as an executable, and convert a file-based app into a full project using `dotnet project convert`. A limitation noted is that only single-file conversion is currently supported, with multi-file support planned for .NET 11.

recent_posts.title: Software Engineering 2.0: The Architecture of an Agent
recent_posts.summary: A conceptual walkthrough of a proposed agent architecture framework called 'Software Engineering 2.0', breaking agents into three layers: data (configuration, identity, structure), decision (local/hosted/external LLM), and direction (return, tools, callback). Each layer maps to orchestration services with foundation sub-services underneath, all coordinated by an agent coordination service. The author promotes a spec-driven approach that is language-agnostic, allowing implementation in .NET, Python, Java, or any language. The session also touches on agent-to-agent (A2A) communication and the fractal, composable nature of the architecture.

recent_posts.title: Give credits to your team mates #motivation #leadership #management #appreciation

recent_posts.title: Lead by example using AI
recent_posts.summary: A technical lead shares their perspective on why engineering managers and team leads must personally adopt AI coding tools rather than simply mandating their use. By returning to hands-on coding with tools like Claude Code, the author demonstrates that leading by example is the only effective way to drive AI adoption and productivity improvements across a team.

recent_posts.title: Real-world WPF Modernization Showcase
recent_posts.summary: A real-world walkthrough of migrating the MaterialDesignInXamlToolkit WPF showcase app to Uno Platform using AI Agents. The post covers a structured migration skill that guides agents through XAML dialect differences, control mapping, namespace replacements, and VisualStateManager rewrites. Two migration paths are discussed — in-place and iterative — with the iterative approach chosen for this larger project. Uno Platform's MCP Servers enable agents to interact with the live running UI for validation, replacing guesswork with systematic testing. The result is a cross-platform app running on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and WebAssembly from a single codebase, with the migrated source code available on GitHub.

recent_posts.title: Claude hallucinated .claudeignore and here is what actually works
recent_posts.summary: Claude Code does not support a .claudeignore file — Claude hallucinated this feature, and the misinformation spread widely across blogs, Stack Overflow, and wikis. Developers who added .claudeignore files believing they were protecting secrets were getting no protection at all. The actual mechanism in Claude Code is permissions.deny in .claude/settings.json, but this only restricts the Read tool, not Glob or Grep. GitHub Copilot has a content exclusion feature but it requires Business/Enterprise tier and doesn't apply to agent workflows. OpenAI Codex has no built-in exclusion mechanism. For .NET projects, .gitignore provides broader coverage for build artifacts, while the real security answer is never storing credentials in the repository in the first place.
